```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

summary_cache <- fromJSON("viceroyalty_of_new_spain_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
reg_spec <- read_json5_clean("viceroyalty_of_new_spain.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("viceroyalty_of_new_spain_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("viceroyalty_of_new_spain_source_ledger.json5")

clean_label <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Intendencia de Mexico", "Intendencia de México", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Michoacan", "Michoacán", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("San Luis Potosi", "San Luis Potosí", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Merida", "Mérida", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Yucatan", "Yucatán", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Nuevo Leon", "Nuevo León", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\\\\", "", s)
  trimws(s)
}

regions_doc <- reg_spec$regions
subregions_grid <- summary_cache$subregions

reg_lookup <- setNames(
  vapply(regions_doc, function(r) clean_label(r$name), character(1)),
  vapply(regions_doc, function(r) r$id, character(1))
)

n_sites <- as.integer(summary_cache$settlement_stats$total_settlements)
n_excluded <- as.integer(ledger_data$total_excluded)
doc_area <- sum(vapply(regions_doc, function(r) as.numeric(r$area_km2), numeric(1)))
grid_area <- as.numeric(summary_cache$area_km2)

doc_tot <- function(yr) {
  sum(vapply(regions_doc, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[as.character(yr)]]), numeric(1)))
}
```

# Abstract

Between the creation of the Viceroyalty of New Spain under Antonio de Mendoza in 1535 and the achievement of Mexican independence in 1821, colonial Mexico passed through the deepest demographic contraction in Mesoamerican history before mounting a sustained, spatially transformative recovery. Across 12 Bourbon intendancies and northern frontier provinces covering 1.890.006 km² on the administrative vector footprint (1.965.350 km² on the continuous gridded mask), documentary regional benchmarks trace an initial decline from 3,67M (3.665.000, compared with Gonzalo Aguirre Beltrán's classic 1570 viceregal tally of 3,38M) to a mid-seventeenth-century nadir of 2,09M (2.085.000) in 1646 following recurring *cocoliztli* and smallpox epidemics [@AguirreBeltran1946; @CookBorah1971; @Fernandez2023Epidemias]. Recovery gathered pace after 1650, lifting the viceregal population to 3,23M (3.230.000) in José Antonio de Villaseñor y Sánchez's 1742 *Theatro Americano* horizon, 4,53M (4.534.094, aligning with the 4,48M enumerated across the 12 intendancies and frontier in the 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo Census) and 5,90M (5.895.700, closely tracking Alexander von Humboldt's 1803 *Ensayo Político* adjustment of 5,84M) before the 1810 to 1821 War of Independence checked late-colonial momentum at roughly 6,53M (6.525.000) in 1821 [@Gerhard1962; @SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811]. On the conservative spatial-kriging substratum (1600 to 1820), aggregate population rose from 1,78M to 4,57M, registering a sharp 1810 insurgency dip from 4,25M to 4,08M. Crucially, recovery redrew Mexico's human geography: whereas the central highlands of México, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Oaxaca remained populous, the fastest expansion shifted north-westward into the silver-mining and commercial grain belt of the Bajío (Guanajuato rising 6,41-fold from 85k in 1646 to 545k in 1821, reaching 17,36 inhabitants per km² on documentary benchmarks and 10,05 on the 1820 grid) and Nueva Galicia. Supported by 826 catalogued colonial settlements led by Mexico City (179,8k), Guanajuato (70,6k), Puebla (67,8k) and Guadalajara (40k), this chapter reconstructs New Spain's intendancy demography, urban hierarchy, *casta* composition and subsistence crises across nearly three centuries of imperial rule.

# Background

## Imperial Consolidation, Congregaciones and the Demographic Nadir (1535 to 1650)

When Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza entered Mexico City in November 1535 to replace the chaotic rule of the first *Audiencias*, New Spain was an archipelago of Spanish municipal islands floating inside an overwhelmingly indigenous sea. The imperial state inherited the dense agrarian corridors of the Basin of Mexico, the Puebla-Tlaxcala valley, highland Michoacán and the valleys of Oaxaca, yet its fiscal machinery rested on an indigenous population already reeling from virgin-soil epidemics [@Gibson1964; @Mccaa1999Siglo]. First smallpox in 1520, then measles in 1531 and finally the devastating haemorrhagic *cocoliztli* outbreaks of 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1581 cut swathes through central Mexican villages [@CookBorah1971; @Fernandez2023Epidemias]. Modern non-quantitative and fiscal-tribute reassessments confirm that whether one places the 1519 pre-conquest baseline at conservative or high levels, the sixteenth-century demographic loss was catastrophic in both absolute mortality and institutional shock [@Mccaa1999Siglo; @Fernandez2023Epidemias].

Spanish administrators responded to collapsing village populations with aggressive spatial engineering. Under Viceroys Luis de Velasco and the Count of Monterrey between 1550 and 1605, the Crown ordered repeated *congregaciones* (forced nucleated resettlements) that swept dispersed highland hamlets into gridded *cabeceras* centred on parish churches [@Gerhard1993; @Gibson1964]. Official decrees framed *congregación* as evangelical instruction and rationalised tribute collection, yet its demographic side effects were severe. Concentrating weakened families into tighter housing accelerated pathogen transmission during late-sixteenth-century fevers, while detaching cultivators from dispersed hillside micro-plots eroded subsistence buffers [@Zevallos1999Movimento; @Ross1953Studies]. Many indigenous households answered tribute arrears and forced *repartimiento* labour drafts simply by voting with their feet, fleeing home *pueblos de indios* into urban *barrios*, northern mining camps or private Spanish estates where personal status blurred and village head taxes were harder to enforce [@Zevallos1999Movimento; @Gibson1964].

By the mid-seventeenth century, New Spain reached its colonial demographic floor. Between 1570 and 1646, our documentary regional series drops from 3,67M to 2,09M inhabitants—a contraction of 43,1% even after the worst of the initial post-conquest mortality had passed [@CookBorah1971; @AguirreBeltran1946]. In the core intendancies of México, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Oaxaca, populations roughly halved across those seven decades, leaving abandoned agricultural terraces around Lake Texcoco, Mixteca Alta and Tlaxcala to be absorbed by expanding Spanish wheat haciendas and sheep *estancias* [@Gibson1964; @Porras1994Poblacio]. Along the tropical Gulf lowlands of Veracruz and the coastal plains of Colima and Tabasco, the indigenous collapse was even more complete, turning fertile riverine basins into thinly peopled cattle ranges and creating acute labour shortages that Spanish planters filled through the transatlantic African slave trade [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993].

## Silver Frontiers, Bajío Estates and Post-1650 Demographic Recovery

Even as the indigenous heartland shrank toward its 1646 nadir, an entirely different colonial Mexico was rising north of the Lerma River. The discovery of rich silver lodes at Zacatecas in 1546, Guanajuato in 1554, San Luis Potosí in 1592 and Parral in 1631 drew Spanish prospectors, Tlaxcalan colonists, Purépecha artisans, Afro-Mexican muleteers and mixed-ancestry wage labourers onto the semi-arid Chichimec steppe [@Brading1971; @Collhurtado1999Mineri; @MinoGrijalva2001]. Following the brutal Chichimec War (1550 to 1590), Crown peacemaking settled allied Tlaxcalan families in northern *pueblos* from San Luis Potosí to Saltillo, creating a permanent agrarian scaffolding behind the fortified *presidios* and Franciscan or Jesuit missions [@Gerhard1993; @Ross1953Studies].

To feed the northern *reales de minas*, supply tallow, leather, draught mules and mercury-amalgamation mills, a vast agro-industrial corridor took shape across the Bajío—the fertile alluvial basin linking Querétaro, Celaya, Salamanca, Irapuato, Silao, León and San Miguel el Grande [@Brading1971; @MinoGrijalva2001]. Unlike the Valley of Mexico or Oaxaca, where entrenched communal villages (*repúblicas de indios*) retained legal title to ancestral lands, the Bajío was largely colonised after 1550 by free wage labourers (*laboríos*), sharecroppers and mixed-ancestry rancheros working commercial wheat and maize haciendas alongside textile workshops (*obrajes*) [@Brading1971; @Ross1953Studies]. Because mining wages in Guanajuato and Zacatecas outstripped central highland earnings, the Bajío acted as a demographic magnet for two centuries.

After 1650, New Spain's long demographic decline reversed decisively. Gradually acquired herd immunity among indigenous cohorts to Old World childhood pathogens—combined with steady natural increase among creole, mestizo and Afro-Mexican populations—lifted aggregate headcounts from 2,09M in 1646 to 3,23M by 1742 [@CookBorah1971; @Gerhard1962; @RabellRomero1990]. Recovery was strikingly uneven in geography. Between 1646 and 1742, the old Mesoamerican cores of México (+53,4%), Puebla-Tlaxcala (+48,4%) and Oaxaca (+51,2%) regained roughly half their mid-seventeenth-century losses, whereas Guanajuato surged 2,59-fold (from 85k to 220k), Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí doubled (from 85k to 175k) and Guadalajara-Nueva Galicia nearly doubled (from 145k to 285k) [@Gerhard1962; @Sanchez2000Algunas; @Collhurtado1999Mineri]. By the middle of the eighteenth century, silver production had entered its Bourbon super-cycle, quadrupling mintage at the Mexico City Casa de Moneda between 1700 and 1805 and turning the Valenciana vein at Guanajuato into the single richest silver mine on earth [@Brading1971; @Ficker2025Mineri].

## Casta Hierarchies, Mestizaje and Afro-Mexican Populations

Colonial New Spain was neither a simple transplant of Castile nor an unchanged indigenous continuity; it became the Americas' largest laboratory of biological and cultural admixture. Spanish legal theory originally sought to divide the realm into two separate corporations—a *república de españoles* governed by urban *cabildos* and a *república de indios* organised into self-governing communal towns with *cajas de comunidad*—yet demographic reality shattered that binary within two generations [@Ross1953Studies; @Rankinanaya2022Mexico]. By 1570, Gonzalo Aguirre Beltrán's classic ethnic breakdown enumerated roughly 3,34M indigenous people alongside barely 6,6k Europeans, 20,6k enslaved and free Africans and 11,1k mestizos and mulatos [@AguirreBeltran1946]. Over the next two centuries, the proportion of non-indigenous and mixed-ancestry inhabitants climbed steadily, reshaping both cities and commercial hinterlands.

Afro-Mexicans played a demographic role far larger than nineteenth-century national myths acknowledged. Between 1519 and 1650, roughly 110k to 150k enslaved Africans entered New Spain through Veracruz and Campeche, outnumbering European immigrants during the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries [@AguirreBeltran1946]. They laboured in the sugar plantations of Morelos (Cuernavaca and Cuautla), Jalapa, Córdoba and Orizaba, in the silver mines of Taxco, Pachuca, Zacatecas and Parral, on coastal cattle ranches from Veracruz to Guerrero and as artisans and domestic servants across Mexico City, Puebla and Guadalajara [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Lausana2015Marginalidad]. Simultaneously, the Manila Galleon trade linking Acapulco to Cavite brought thousands of Filipino, Malay and South Asian sailors, artisans and enslaved *chinos* onto Mexico's Pacific littoral, leaving a measurable genomic signal in western and coastal Guerrero and Michoacán populations documented by modern admixture studies [@Rodriguezrodriguez2021Admixture].

By the late eighteenth century, parish registers and the 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo Census recorded an intricate *sistema de castas* distinguishing *españoles* (both peninsular *gachupines* and American-born *criollos*), *indios*, *mestizos*, *mulatos*, *pardos*, *lobos* and *coyotes* [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Bustamante1991Matter; @Healy2017Social]. Yet archival micro-studies from both the urban core and northern frontier show that *casta* labels were socially negotiated rather than genetically fixed. An individual baptized as a *mulato* or *mestizo* could marry or be buried as a *coyote* or *español* depending on occupation, wealth, tribute exemption and local reputation [@Bustamante1991Matter; @Lausana2015Marginalidad; @Healy2017Social]. Even so, broad regional proportions remained unmistakable around 1803: indigenous people still comprised roughly 60% of New Spain's total population (rising above 80% in Oaxaca and Yucatán and roughly 65% to 70% in Puebla and rural México), Europeans and creoles accounted for roughly 18% to 20% and mixed-ancestry *castas*—mestizos, mulatos and pardos combined—made up 20% to 22%, reaching clear majorities in the mining centres of Guanajuato, Zacatecas and the northern presidial towns [@Humboldt1811; @AguirreBeltran1946; @MinoGrijalva2001].

## Bourbon Intendancies, Subsistence Crises and the War of Independence (1736 to 1821)

Under the Bourbon monarchs Charles III and Charles IV, Madrid overhauled New Spain's fragmented patchwork of nearly 200 *alcaldías mayores* and *corregimientos*. The 1786 *Real Ordenanza de Intendentes* consolidated the viceroyalty into 12 provincial intendancies—México, Puebla (with Tlaxcala detached as a separate *gobierno* in 1793), Veracruz, Oaxaca, Valladolid (Michoacán), Guanajuato, Guadalajara, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Mérida (Yucatán), Durango and Arizpe (Sonora-Sinaloa)—flanked by the militarised *Provincias Internas* of the north and the Californias [@Gerhard1993; @Rankinanaya2022Mexico]. Fiscal reform accompanied administrative reorganisation: Crown monopolies on tobacco and gunpowder, stricter *alcabala* sales taxes and tighter tribute audits doubled viceregal revenues while generating the statistical surveys—above all Viceroy Revillagigedo's 1790 to 1793 census—on which colonial historical demography rests [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca].

Eighteenth-century growth was nonetheless punctuated by brutal Malthusian subsistence and epidemiological shocks. The worst epidemic of the late colonial era struck between 1736 and 1739, when *matlazáhuatl* (generally identified as epidemic typhus or viral haemorrhagic fever) swept outward from a textile mill in Tacuba across the Basin of Mexico, Puebla, the Bajío and western Mexico, killing an estimated 40k residents in Mexico City alone and perhaps 150k to 200k across central New Spain [@RabellRomero1990; @MinoGrijalva2001; @Sanchez2000Algunas]. Scarcely a generation after the 1779 to 1780 smallpox pandemic, early frosts in August 1785 destroyed maize harvests across the central plateau, triggering the infamous *Año del Hambre* (Year of Hunger) of 1785 to 1786 [@Brading1971; @RabellRomero1990]. As maize prices trebled and destitute rural families poured into Guanajuato, León, Guadalajara and Mexico City in search of charity soup kitchens, starvation and typhus claimed an estimated 300k lives—roughly 6% to 7% of the entire viceroyalty—and exposed the fragility of an agrarian economy where hacienda expansion had squeezed communal maize reserves [@Brading1971; @Sanchez2000Algunas; @Porras1994Poblacio].

Those structural tensions detonated in September 1810, when Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the *Grito de Dolores* in the very heart of the Intendancy of Guanajuato. For eleven years (1810 to 1821), insurgent campaigns under Hidalgo, José María Morelos and Vicente Guerrero clashed with royalist armies across the Bajío, Michoacán, Guadalajara, Puebla and the southern Tierra Caliente [@Rankinanaya2022Mexico; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca]. Flooded shafts and capital flight crippled silver output—Guanajuato's urban population plunged by nearly half from 70,6k in 1803 to 35,7k by 1820—while war mortality, military levies, disrupted grain transport and the 1813 typhus epidemic slowed viceregal population growth sharply [@Ficker2025Mineri; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca]. Between 1793 and 1803, New Spain had been adding roughly 2,6% per year on combined enumeration-adjusted baselines (or roughly 1,2% to 1,5% per annum in underlying natural growth once Revillagigedo's under-enumeration is removed); between 1803 and 1821, compound annual growth fell to barely 0,56% across the viceroyalty, leaving an independent Mexico of 6,53M people with ruined mines, fractured fiscal networks and stark regional scars [@Humboldt1811; @Ficker2025Mineri; @Rankinanaya2022Mexico].

# Methodology

## Territorial Architecture of the Twelve Intendancies and Frontier Provinces

To reconcile colonial tax rolls, Bourbon intendancy censuses and spatial demographic surfaces within stable boundaries across 1535 to 1821, this chapter partitions the Viceroyalty of New Spain (within its core Mexican territorial frame) into 12 sub-regional administrative polygons matching the 1786 *Real Ordenanza de Intendentes* and the northern *Provincias Internas* [@Gerhard1993]. Because the northern frontier provinces of Alta California, Nuevo México and Texas lay sparsely populated beyond the primary Mexican core and fall outside the Mexico chapter mask footprint, the 12 territorial units span 1.890.006 km² on the clean historical GIS vector boundary (1.965.349,5 km² on the gridded raster mask, a 3,99% coastline and projection discrepancy).

The 12 regional partitions group four broad ecological and economic zones. First, the densely settled Mesoamerican highland core comprises the Intendencia de México (130.620 km² vector; 133.383 km² grid, stretching from Acapulco through the Basin of Mexico and Toluca to Querétaro and the Huasteca), the Intendencia de Puebla and Gobierno de Tlaxcala (48.178 km² vector; 49.076,5 km² grid) and the Intendencia de Oaxaca (89.492 km² vector; 96.221,2 km² grid). Second, the western and Bajío growth corridor unites the compact Intendencia de Guanajuato (31.401 km² vector; 31.188,6 km² grid), the Intendencia de Valladolid or Michoacán (75.820 km² vector; 77.867,9 km² grid, including Colima) and the Intendencia de Guadalajara or Nueva Galicia (116.928 km² vector; 120.066,9 km² grid, including Aguascalientes and Nayarit). Third, the tropical Gulf littoral and Maya southeast encompass the Intendencia de Veracruz (68.563 km² vector; 73.115,1 km² grid) and the Intendencia de Mérida covering Yucatán and Tabasco (155.912 km² vector; 167.512 km² grid). Fourth, the vast northern mining plateau and arid frontier consist of the combined Intendencias de Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí (129.242 km² vector; 128.410,4 km² grid), the Intendencia de Durango or Nueva Vizcaya (383.074 km² vector; 381.498,3 km² grid, spanning Durango and Chihuahua), the Intendencia de Arizpe covering Sonora-Sinaloa together with Baja California (368.878 km² vector; 408.887,6 km² grid) and the Provincias Internas de Oriente comprising Coahuila, Nuevo León and Nuevo Santander (291.898 km² vector; 298.122,2 km² grid) [@Gerhard1993; @Humboldt1811].

## Archival Enumerations, Tribute Multipliers and Spatial Reconciliation

Colonial Mexican demography relies on three sequential classes of documentary sources, each demanding explicit demographic conversion before sub-regional series can be compared across 1535 to 1821. For the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (1570 and 1646 benchmarks), regional headcounts rest primarily on *tasaciones de tributos* (indigenous tribute rolls) and episcopal *relaciones*, supplemented by fiscal counts of Spanish *vecinos* and Afro-Mexican inhabitants [@CookBorah1971; @AguirreBeltran1946; @Fernandez2023Epidemias]. Because colonial tribute assessments registered *tributarios* (adult married indigenous men, with widows and unmarried adults counted as half-tributaries), total indigenous population $P_{\mathrm{ind}}$ in jurisdiction $r$ at benchmark $t$ is derived via a demographic multiplier $m(t)$:

$$P_{\mathrm{ind},r}(t) = T_r(t) \cdot m(t) \cdot (1 + \epsilon_r)$$

where $T_r(t)$ denotes full tributary units, $m(t)$ ranges between 3,3 and 4,2 persons per tributary depending on post-epidemic age structure (falling near 2,8 to 3,3 immediately after major *cocoliztli* shocks when fertility collapsed and climbing toward 4,0 to 4,5 during eighteenth-century expansion) and $\epsilon_r \in [0,05, 0,15]$ adjusts for tribute-exempt nobles (*caciques*), aged residents and unregistered migrants [@CookBorah1971; @Fernandez2023Epidemias; @Zevallos1999Movimento]. For the 1742 *Theatro Americano* benchmark compiled by Villaseñor y Sánchez and systematically audited by Peter Gerhard, family counts (*familias*) across *indios*, *españoles* and *castas* are converted using regionally calibrated household sizes of 4,2 to 5,0 persons per family [@Gerhard1962; @RabellRomero1990].

For the late Bourbon era, the 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo Census provides New Spain's first nominal household enumeration, yet returns were never fully compiled for Guadalajara, Veracruz and Coahuila, while military-conscription fears prompted widespread evasion [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca; @Cervantescortes2021Registro]. In his 1803 *Ensayo Político*, Alexander von Humboldt reconciled the surviving 1793 intendancy schedules (4.367.703 across the 12 core intendancies, rising to roughly 4,48M to 4,53M with Tlaxcala and frontier districts) by applying an under-enumeration correction factor $\kappa \approx 1,10$ to $1,15$ and projecting a decade of natural surplus derived from parish baptism-to-burial ratios ($B_r / D_r \approx 1,70$ to $2,00$ in non-crisis years):

$$P_r(1803) = \kappa \cdot P_r^{\mathrm{Rev}}(1793) \cdot \left(1 + g_r\right)^{10}$$

where $g_r$ captures annual net natural growth between 1793 and 1803 [@Humboldt1811; @RabellRomero1990; @Porras1994Poblacio]. Inter-benchmark compound annual growth rates across all documentary horizons ($t_1$ to $t_2$) follow standard geometric compounding:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Alongside the six-horizon documentary intendancy ledger (1570, 1646, 1742, 1793, 1803 and 1821), this study integrates a continuous decadal spatial-kriging substratum from 1600 to 1820 (calibrated to 10-year intervals from 1700 onward across the 1.965.350 km² raster mask). Pairing both series explicitly rather than forcing artificial identity exposes where gridded historical land-use models lag behind colonial archival enumerations—most notably in late-Bourbon demographic magnitude and around the 1780 intendancy re-weighting step—while preserving continuous sub-provincial spatial allocation.

## Settlement Gazetteer Compilation and Provenance Auditing

Complementing the intendancy aggregates, this chapter assembles a geocoded settlement gazetteer of `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` colonial Mexican towns, cities, mining *reales*, *pueblos de indios* and frontier missions active between 1535 and 1821. Source-ledger auditing evaluated 859 candidate entries across four sequential ingestion waves: Wave 1 ingested 753 core records from official statistical compilations and colonial archival registers (principally the HGIS de las Indias gazetteer compiled by Werner Stangl alongside INEGI's 2014 *Estadísticas Históricas de México*); Wave 2 added 54 entries from peer-reviewed historical demography monographs (marginal gain 7,17%); Wave 3 added 12 longitudinal backfill series (marginal gain 1,49%); and Wave 4 executed a regional gap-verification sweep adding 7 final nodes (marginal gain 0,85%, confirming corpus saturation below the 1% threshold).

Spatial deduplication and boundary vetting removed `r viscount_fmt_number(n_excluded, 0L)` candidate records: 31 duplicate aliases of major cities already anchored by multi-source series and 2 outer Pimería Alta mission nodes (Tucson and San Xavier) lying north of the chapter's Sonora boundary. All 826 retained settlements carry WGS84 coordinates, a sub-regional intendancy assignment, an explicit primary provenance string and strictly city-proper municipal or parish scope, with a 0% crowd-sourced share. Primary colonial registers inside HGIS de las Indias account for 774 entries on their own—dominated by Bishop Pedro Tamarón y Romeral's 1765 episcopal visitation of Durango and Sonora-Sinaloa (419 records), Ernest Sánchez Santiró's 1778 Archdiocese of México parish padrones (242 records), Archivo General de Indias mission lists for Guadalajara and the north-west (131 records), the 1780 Guadalajara diocesan survey (80 records) and Francisco R. de la Torre Curiel's Sonora mission registers (70 records)—while 52 major colonial cities combine multi-benchmark Revillagigedo, Humboldt, Villaseñor, Gerhard and INEGI longitudinal series [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811; @Gerhard1962; @Gerhard1993].

# Testing and Validation

## Cross-Checks Against Colonial Enumerations and Regional Historiography

Validating New Spain's colonial trajectory requires triangulating our intendancy totals against both eighteenth-century fiscal-ecclesiastical censuses and modern regional demographic reconstructions. At our opening 1570 documentary benchmark, the sum across all 12 sub-regions stands at 3,67M (3.665.000), sitting 8,4% above Aguirre Beltrán's classic 1570 colonial aggregate of 3,38M (3.380.012) because our provincial series incorporates northern frontier indigenous populations across Nueva Vizcaya (130k), Sonora-Sinaloa (165k) and the eastern frontier (75k) that sixteenth-century central Mexican tribute rolls systematically omitted [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993; @Fernandez2023Epidemias]. By 1646, our 2,09M nadir aligns tightly with Cook and Borah's central Mexican trough and Aguirre Beltrán's mid-seventeenth-century count (roughly 1,7M to 2,1M depending on frontier inclusion), reflecting a devastating 43,1% contraction over 76 years [@CookBorah1971; @AguirreBeltran1946; @Mccaa1999Siglo].

For the eighteenth-century recovery, cross-checking against regional monograph series confirms strong internal consistency. In 1742, our 3,23M total matches Gerhard's recalculation of Villaseñor y Sánchez's *Theatro Americano* (roughly 3,2M to 3,3M once non-tributary *castas* and frontier missions are included) [@Gerhard1962; @MinoGrijalva2001]. In 1793, the 12 regional polygons sum to 4,53M (4.534.094), closely matching the 4,48M Revillagigedo viceregal benchmark (the small 1,1% excess reflecting inclusion of Tlaxcala's 60,9k inhabitants alongside Baja California and the eastern *Provincias Internas*) [@SPPRevillagigedo1977]. Regional case studies corroborate individual intendancies: Agustín Grajales Porras's parish-level study of late-colonial Puebla aligns with our 627,4k (1793) to 813,3k (1803) trajectory [@Porras1994Poblacio]; Oziel Talavera Ibarra's collation of the 1790 Revillagigedo returns for Michoacán against Juan José Martínez de Lejarza's 1822 statistical analysis confirms Valladolid's growth from 289,3k in 1793 to 376,4k in 1803 and roughly 420k by Independence [@Hidalgo2024Michoaca]; and Lilia V. Oliver Sánchez's western Mexican reconstructions substantiate Guadalajara's rapid climb from 485k in 1793 to 630,5k in 1803 [@Sanchez2000Algunas].

At the closing 1803 and 1821 horizons, our 1803 documentary sum of 5,90M (5.895.700) tracks Alexander von Humboldt's published estimate of 5,84M (5.837.100) within 1,0%—the minor difference arising from frontier provincial adjustments in Arizpe and the eastern *Provincias Internas* [@Humboldt1811]. Between 1803 and 1821, our 6,53M (6.525.000) Independence-era figure registers the war-induced deceleration noted by political-economic and mining historians, matching early republican estimates of 6,2M to 6,6M made by Fernando Navarro y Noriega and the first post-independence ministries [@Ficker2025Mineri; @Rankinanaya2022Mexico; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca].

## Intendancy Benchmarks and Gridded Substratum Reconciliation

Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} presents the documentary population series across all 12 Bourbon intendancies and frontier provinces from 1570 to 1821, together with 1821 territorial densities and post-nadir recovery multiples (1646 to 1821). Every sub-region displays historically coherent dynamics: severe contraction from 1570 to 1646 across the Mesoamerican core, modest frontier resilience in Guanajuato and Zacatecas-San Luis Potosí, broad eighteenth-century expansion and sharp regional divergence by Independence.

```{r tab-subregion-benchmarks, results='asis'}
doc_rows <- lapply(regions_doc, function(r) {
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p1570 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1570"]])
  p1646 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1646"]])
  p1742 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1742"]])
  p1793 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1793"]])
  p1803 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1803"]])
  p1821 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1821"]])
  d1821 <- if (a > 0) p1821 / a else 0
  mult <- if (p1646 > 0) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(p1821 / p1646, 2L), "x") else "-"
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(a), 0L),
    P1570 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1570),
    P1646 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1646),
    P1742 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1742),
    P1793 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1793),
    P1803 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1803),
    P1821 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1821),
    Dens21 = viscount_fmt_number(d1821, 2L),
    Mult = mult,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_doc <- do.call(rbind, doc_rows)
df_doc_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Viceroyalty Total (12 Units)",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(doc_area), 0L),
  P1570 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1570)),
  P1646 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1646)),
  P1742 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1742)),
  P1793 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1793)),
  P1803 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1803)),
  P1821 = viscount_fmt_pop(doc_tot(1821)),
  Dens21 = viscount_fmt_number(doc_tot(1821) / doc_area, 2L),
  Mult = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(doc_tot(1821) / doc_tot(1646), 2L), "x"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_doc <- rbind(df_doc, df_doc_tot)
rownames(df_doc) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_doc,
  "Documentary population benchmarks across 12 Bourbon intendancies and northern frontier provinces, 1570 to 1821, with 1821 density (inhabitants per km²) and post-1646 recovery multiples.",
  c("Intendancy or Province", "Area (km²)", "1570", "1646", "1742", "1793", "1803", "1821", "1821 Dens.", "1646-1821"),
  list(label = "tab:subregion-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Direct comparison of the two foundational late-colonial statistical monuments—the 1793 Revillagigedo Census and Humboldt's 1803 *Ensayo Político* intendancy tables—appears in Table \ref{tab:hgis-intendancies}, compiled straight from the chapter's harmonised sub-administrative archival ledger [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811]. Across all 12 core intendancies, enumerated totals rise from 4.367.703 in 1793 to 5.775.200 in 1803 (+32,2% overall), while the full viceregal aggregate (incorporating frontier provinces) climbs from 3.380.012 in 1570 to 5.837.100 in 1803. Notice that the uniform roughly 30% decadal uplift across México (+30,0%), Guadalajara (+30,0%), Oaxaca (+30,0%), Guanajuato (+30,0%), Mérida (+30,0%), Valladolid (+30,1%), Durango (+30,0%), Veracruz (+30,0%), Zacatecas (+29,9%) and Sonora (+30,0%) directly reflects Humboldt's transparent methodological rule: adding 10% to 15% for Revillagigedo under-registration plus roughly 15% to 18% for ten years of natural increase, whereas Puebla's steeper 43,6% jump (from 566.443 to 813.300) incorporates the re-inclusion of Tlaxcala's roughly 60k inhabitants into Humboldt's 1803 table [@Humboldt1811; @Porras1994Poblacio].

```{r tab-hgis-intendancies, results='asis'}
hgis_tbl <- summary_cache$hgis_subadmin_table
int_rows_1793 <- Filter(function(x) identical(x$level, "intendancy") && as.integer(x$year) == 1793L, hgis_tbl)
int_rows_1803 <- Filter(function(x) identical(x$level, "intendancy") && as.integer(x$year) == 1803L, hgis_tbl)
agg_1570 <- Filter(function(x) identical(x$level, "viceroyalty") && as.integer(x$year) == 1570L, hgis_tbl)[[1]]
agg_1803 <- Filter(function(x) identical(x$level, "viceroyalty") && as.integer(x$year) == 1803L, hgis_tbl)[[1]]

map_1803 <- setNames(
  vapply(int_rows_1803, function(x) as.numeric(x$population), numeric(1)),
  vapply(int_rows_1803, function(x) as.character(x$unit_code), character(1))
)

tot_1793_int <- sum(vapply(int_rows_1793, function(x) as.numeric(x$population), numeric(1)))
tot_1803_int <- sum(vapply(int_rows_1803, function(x) as.numeric(x$population), numeric(1)))

h_rows <- lapply(int_rows_1793, function(x) {
  uc <- as.character(x$unit_code)
  p93 <- as.numeric(x$population)
  p03 <- if (uc %in% names(map_1803)) map_1803[[uc]] else NA_real_
  chg <- if (!is.na(p03) && p93 > 0) paste0("+", viscount_fmt_number(100 * (p03 - p93) / p93, 1L), "%") else "-"
  sh03 <- if (!is.na(p03)) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * p03 / tot_1803_int, 1L), "%") else "-"
  data.frame(
    Unit = clean_label(x$unit_name),
    Rev1793 = viscount_fmt_number(p93, 0L),
    Hum1803 = viscount_fmt_number(p03, 0L),
    Change = chg,
    Share03 = sh03,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_hgis <- do.call(rbind, h_rows)
df_hgis <- rbind(
  df_hgis,
  data.frame(
    Unit = "Twelve Core Intendancies Subtotal",
    Rev1793 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1793_int, 0L),
    Hum1803 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1803_int, 0L),
    Change = paste0("+", viscount_fmt_number(100 * (tot_1803_int - tot_1793_int) / tot_1793_int, 1L), "%"),
    Share03 = "100%",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  data.frame(
    Unit = "Viceroyalty Aggregate (1570 / 1803 Benchmarks)",
    Rev1793 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(agg_1570$population), 0L), " (1570)"),
    Hum1803 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(agg_1803$population), 0L),
    Change = paste0("+", viscount_fmt_number(100 * (as.numeric(agg_1803$population) - as.numeric(agg_1570$population)) / as.numeric(agg_1570$population), 1L), "%"),
    Share03 = "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
)
rownames(df_hgis) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_hgis,
  "Bourbon intendancy enumerations from the 1793 Revillagigedo Census and Alexander von Humboldt's 1803 statistical tables, plus the 1570 and 1803 viceregal aggregates.",
  c("Administrative Unit", "1793 Revillagigedo", "1803 Humboldt", "Change", "1803 Share"),
  list(label = "tab:hgis-intendancies", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Testing the documentary series against the gridded spatial substratum (tabulated in Appendix Table \ref{tab:gridded-trajectory}) yields an instructive diagnostic. In 1740 to 1750, the gridded substratum (3,13M to 3,32M) matches Villaseñor's 1742 documentary total (3,23M) almost identically. By 1790 to 1800, however, the gridded surface stands at 3,79M to 4,25M—roughly 15% to 28% below the Revillagigedo (4,53M) and Humboldt (5,84M to 5,90M) archival benchmarks—and reaches 4,57M in 1820 compared with 6,53M on documentary projections. That divergence reflects a well-known property of conservative continental land-use models: they track seventeenth-century recovery smoothly and capture the 1810 war shock (dipping from 4,25M in 1800 to 4,08M in 1810), yet under-allocate the explosive late-eighteenth-century urban and rural intensification of central and western Mexico.

# Results

## Viceregal Demographic Trajectory from Consolidation to Independence

Across the nearly three centuries from 1535 to 1821, colonial Mexico's demographic trajectory describes an asymmetric V-shaped trough followed by a surging late-Bourbon climb and a wartime plateau. On our archival intendancy benchmarks, population fell from 3,67M in 1570 to its 1646 nadir of 2,09M (a compound decline of -0,74% per annum across 76 years), then rebounded steadily at +0,46% per annum to 3,23M in 1742, accelerated to +0,67% per annum between 1742 and 1793 (4,53M) and surged across the final pre-insurgency decade before slowing to +0,56% per annum between 1803 (5,90M) and Independence in 1821 (6,53M). Over the entire 175-year post-nadir recovery (1646 to 1821), the viceroyalty multiplied 3,13-fold, lifting mean viceregal density from 1,10 inhabitants per km² in 1646 to 3,45 inhabitants per km² in 1821.

Figure \ref{fig:new-spain-trajectory} illustrates the continuous gridded decadal surface from 1600 to 1820 (Panel A) alongside sub-regional gridded densities in 1820 (Panel B). On the gridded curve, aggregate population climbs from 1,78M in 1600 to 3,30M in 1700, undergoes an early-eighteenth-century setback to 2,93M in 1710 before recovering past 3,32M in 1750, dips modestly during the mid-century subsistence stress of 1760 (3,17M) and then climbs briskly through 1780 (3,60M), 1790 (3,79M) and 1800 (4,25M). Crucially, Panel A captures the demographic shock of the 1810 insurgency directly, dipping 3,8% to 4,08M before rebounding to 4,57M by 1820. Equally revealing is Panel B's density ranking: by 1820, the compact Intendencia de Guanajuato leads the entire viceroyalty at 10,05 inhabitants per km² on the gridded surface (and 17,36 inhabitants per km² on documentary 1821 benchmarks), overtaking even the Intendencia de México (7,06 gridded; 12,86 documentary) and Puebla-Tlaxcala (6,28 gridded; 18,27 documentary).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/viceroyalty_of_new_spain_population_trajectory.png",
  "Gridded decadal population trajectory for the Viceroyalty of New Spain and leading sub-regions from 1600 to 1820 (Panel A) and sub-regional population density rankings in 1820 (Panel B).",
  "fig:new-spain-trajectory"
)
```

Behind those headline figures lies a profound northward and westward shift in Mexico's demographic centre of gravity. In 1570, the three old Mesoamerican highland cores of México, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Oaxaca contained 2,19M inhabitants—59,8% of the entire viceroyalty—whereas the Bajío, western Mexico and northern mining belt (Guanajuato, Guadalajara, Zacatecas-San Luis Potosí, Durango, Arizpe and the eastern *Provincias Internas*) held just 820k (22,4%). By 1821, although the central-southern core had recovered to 3,14M, its viceregal share had fallen to 48,0%. Meanwhile, Guanajuato, Guadalajara and Zacatecas-San Luis Potosí alone expanded nearly fivefold from 315k in 1646 to 1,74M in 1821 (26,6% of New Spain), forging the densely settled central-western axis that would dominate modern Mexican politics and economy [@Brading1971; @MinoGrijalva2001; @Contributors2023Adolescence].

## Central Highland Core: México, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Oaxaca

The Intendencia de México (130.620 km² vector; 133.383 km² grid) remained New Spain's demographic anchor throughout the colonial epoch. Dropping by half from 1,15M in 1570 to 580k in 1646 under recurring *cocoliztli* epidemics, lake-drainage labour drafts (*desagüe* of Huehuetoca) and *congregación* relocations [@Gibson1964; @Fernandez2023Epidemias], it rebounded steadily to 890k in 1742, 1,16M (1.162.886) in 1793, 1,51M (1.511.800) in 1803 and 1,68M in 1821—still accounting for 25,7% of the viceroyalty at Independence (12,86 inhabitants per km² documentary; 7,06 on the 1820 grid). Its demographic profile was sharply bifurcated. At its centre sat Mexico City—the largest metropolis in the Western Hemisphere—which grew from 54,2k in 1570 and 52,4k in 1646 to 98k in 1742, 104,8k in 1790, 137k in 1803 and 179,8k by 1820, drawing migrants from across the plateau and sustaining an extensive, often under-recorded urban female labour market in domestic service, tobacco factories (*Real Fábrica de Tabacos*) and street commerce [@Cervantescortes2021Registro; @MinoGrijalva2001]. Surrounding the capital stretched dense indigenous rural districts across the Valley of Toluca (Toluca peaking at 19,8k), Chalco, Xochimilco, Texcoco (14,7k) and the Mezquital (Actopan's parish district at 25,8k in 1778), flanked northward by Querétaro's booming woollen *obrajes* (35k in 1803) and southward by Cuernavaca's sugar estates staffed by Afro-Mexican and indigenous workers [@Gibson1964; @AguirreBeltran1946].

Immediately east across the volcanic sierra, the compact Intendencia de Puebla and Gobierno de Tlaxcala (48.178 km² vector; 49.076,5 km² grid) achieved the highest documentary density in New Spain by 1821 at 18,27 inhabitants per km² (6,28 on the 1820 grid). Contracting from 620k in 1570 to 310k in 1646, Puebla-Tlaxcala recovered to 460k in 1742, 627,4k in 1793 (566.443 in Puebla proper plus Tlaxcala's roughly 61k), 813,3k in 1803 and 880k in 1821 [@Porras1994Poblacio; @Humboldt1811]. Founded in 1531 as an exclusively Spanish agricultural town astride the Veracruz-Mexico City highway, Puebla de los Ángeles grew rapidly into the viceroyalty's premier manufacturing hub for cotton and woollen cloth, soap, glass and Talavera ceramics, reaching 26,8k in 1646, 50,4k in 1742, 56,9k in 1790 and 67,8k in 1803 before royalist-insurgent disruptions and competing European textile imports trimmed it to 60k by 1820 [@MinoGrijalva2001; @Porras1994Poblacio]. Outside the capital, Cholula, Tepeaca, Huejotzingo and autonomous Tlaxcala maintained dense Nahuatl-speaking agricultural communities, while Orizaba (15,8k in 1820) thrived on the Bourbon tobacco monopoly along the temperate eastern escarpment.

South of Puebla, the mountainous Intendencia de Oaxaca (89.492 km² vector; 96.221,2 km² grid) preserved the most overwhelmingly indigenous demography in colonial Mexico. After falling from 420k in 1570 to 215k in 1646, Oaxaca recovered steadily to 325k in 1742, 411,3k in 1793, 534,8k in 1803 and 575k in 1821 (6,43 inhabitants per km² documentary; 4,01 gridded). Unlike central or northern Mexico, where Spanish haciendas alienated large tracts of arable land, Zapotec and Mixtec *repúblicas de indios* retained control of the vast majority of communal valleys and mountain *pueblos*, anchored economically by cochineal dye (*grana cochinilla*)—New Spain's second most valuable export after silver—and hand-woven cotton textiles [@Gerhard1993; @Ross1953Studies]. Because population remained dispersed across hundreds of nucleated rural *pueblos* rather than Spanish cities, Antequera (Oaxaca City, 24k in 1803) stood as the intendancy's sole major urban centre, accounting for less than 5% of provincial population.

## The Bajío and Western Heartland: Guanajuato, Valladolid and Nueva Galicia

No part of New Spain matched the demographic dynamism of the Bajío. The Intendencia de Guanajuato (31.401 km² vector; 31.188,6 km² grid)—the smallest of the 12 provinces in territory—transformed from a contested frontier buffer of 115k in 1570 and 85k in 1646 into the most densely settled industrial-agrarian province of Bourbon Mexico, surging 6,41-fold to 220k in 1742, 397,9k in 1793, 517,3k in 1803 and 545k in 1821 (17,36 inhabitants per km² documentary; 10,05 gridded, first on the 1820 grid) [@Brading1971; @Humboldt1811]. Its silver capital, Guanajuato, expanded from 5,6k in 1600 and 27,5k in 1742 to 70,6k in 1803 (including surrounding mining *reales* along the Veta Madre), overtaking Puebla as New Spain's second city before insurgent warfare and flooded shafts halved it to 35,7k by 1820 [@Brading1971; @Ficker2025Mineri]. Equally important, Guanajuato did not rely on a single primate city: a tight urban constellation of León (21,4k in 1810), San Miguel el Grande (18,2k), Celaya (16,8k) and Irapuato (14,6k) linked irrigated wheat estates, cattle ranches and artisan workshops into a polycentric regional market [@MinoGrijalva2001; @Brading1971].

South-west of the Bajío, the Intendencia de Valladolid or Michoacán (75.820 km² vector; 77.867,9 km² grid) combined the cool Purépecha lake basins around Pátzcuaro and Tzintzuntzan with the hot sugar and indigo valleys of the Balsas Tierra Caliente and Pacific Colima. Declining from 265k in 1570 to 140k in 1646, Michoacán recovered to 225k in 1742, 289,3k in 1793, 376,4k in 1803 and 420k in 1821 (5,54 inhabitants per km² documentary; 4,73 gridded) [@Hidalgo2024Michoaca; @Collhurtado1999Mineri]. Mid-eighteenth-century mining revivals at Tlalpujahua, Angangueo, Ozumatlán and Inguarán stimulated provincial silver and copper extraction across the Bishopric of Michoacán, while Valladolid (modern Morelia) grew modestly to 18k to 21k by 1803 to 1805 as an ecclesiastical, administrative and agrarian capital [@Collhurtado1999Mineri; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca]. Because Michoacán straddled both the Bajío insurgency theatre and Morelos's southern campaigns, Talavera Ibarra's comparison of 1790 Revillagigedo returns against Martínez de Lejarza's 1822 statistical survey highlights severe parish-level disruption in the Tierra Caliente alongside enduring highland resilience [@Hidalgo2024Michoaca].

Further west, the Intendencia de Guadalajara or Nueva Galicia (116.928 km² vector; 120.066,9 km² grid) underwent a sustained 4,79-fold expansion from its 1646 low of 145k to 285k in 1742, 485k in 1793, 630,5k in 1803 and 695k in 1821 (5,94 inhabitants per km² documentary; 4,76 gridded) [@Sanchez2000Algunas; @Humboldt1811]. Founded in 1542 as the seat of its own *Audiencia* and bishopric, Guadalajara evolved from a modest provincial capital of 4,6k in 1570 and 14,5k in 1742 into western Mexico's undisputed commercial metropolis: 24,2k in 1789 to 1793, 32k in 1803 and 40k in 1820, actually gaining migrants during the War of Independence as merchants relocated away from devastated Guanajuato [@Sanchez2000Algunas; @MinoGrijalva2001]. Across the Los Altos plateau northeast of Guadalajara, mixed creole-mestizo ranching parishes such as Lagos (22,2k parish district in 1780), Aguascalientes (20,5k) and Encarnación (19,2k) recorded some of the highest natural fertility rates in late-colonial New Spain [@Sanchez2000Algunas; @RabellRomero1990].

## Gulf Littoral and Maya Southeast: Veracruz and the Intendancy of Mérida

Along the humid Gulf of Mexico coast, the Intendencia de Veracruz (68.563 km² vector; 73.115,1 km² grid) presented a stark epidemiological contrast to the cool central plateau. Because yellow fever (*vómito negro*) and endemic malaria devastated both indigenous lowlands and unacclimatised European arrivals, Veracruz dropped from 145k in 1570 to 75k in 1646 and recovered only slowly to 105k in 1742, 120k in 1793, 156k in 1803 and 185k in 1821 (2,70 inhabitants per km² documentary; 2,84 gridded) [@Gerhard1993; @AguirreBeltran1946]. The walled port of Veracruz—sole Atlantic gateway for the Spanish silver fleets and European merchandise—never exceeded 16k permanent residents in 1803, as wealthy merchants preferred the healthier upland climate of Xalapa (home to the eighteenth-century Atlantic trade fairs) and Córdoba, where Afro-Mexican and *pardo* populations formed a major share of both plantation labour and coastal militia companies [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Lausana2015Marginalidad].

Across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, the Intendencia de Mérida covering Yucatán and Tabasco (155.912 km² vector; 167.512 km² grid) followed a distinct Maya demographic rhythm. Lacking silver mines and rich volcanic soils, colonial Yucatán drew relatively few European settlers; its economy rested on indigenous tribute in cotton cloth (*mantas*), beeswax and maize alongside coastal logwood (*palo de tinte*) and cattle estates [@Farriss1984]. As Nancy Farriss demonstrated, Maya communities cushioned colonial demands through periodic mobility between Spanish-controlled *pueblos* in the north-west and unreduced forest *montaña* refuges in the south-east [@Farriss1984; @Zevallos1999Movimento]. Falling from 245k in 1570 to 185k in 1646—a shallower proportional decline (-24,5%) than central Mexico—Yucatán rebounded steadily to 265k in 1742, 358,3k in 1793, 465,8k in 1803 and 525k in 1821 (3,37 inhabitants per km² documentary; 2,63 gridded), largely spared the direct military devastation of the 1810 to 1821 insurgency. Urban life centred on Mérida (36k in 1820, fifth in the viceroyalty), the fortified port of Campeche (19,5k) and eastern Valladolid Yucatán [@Farriss1984; @Humboldt1811].

## Northern Silver Reales and the Provincias Internas

North of the Tropic of Cancer, arid steppes, desert basins and mobile Apache and Comanche raiding zones held population densities an order of magnitude below central Mexico, yet silver wealth and frontier colonisation drove dramatic proportional growth. Closest to the Bajío, the combined Intendencias de Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí (129.242 km² vector; 128.410,4 km² grid) multiplied 5,82-fold from their 1646 low of 85k to 175k in 1742, 352,1k in 1793, 457,7k in 1803 and 495k in 1821 (3,83 inhabitants per km² documentary; 2,79 gridded) [@Brading1971; @Humboldt1811]. Zacatecas—pioneer silver metropolis of the sixteenth-century north—revived strongly during the late Bourbon boom to reach 33k in 1803 (seventh in New Spain), complemented by San Luis Potosí (19k in 1820), Sierra de Pinos (18,1k district in 1780) and the booming Real de Catorce silver camp discovered in 1778 [@Brading1971; @Ficker2025Mineri].

Beyond Zacatecas stretched the three immense frontier jurisdictions covering over 1,04M km²—more than half of New Spain's land area yet under 8,5% of its 1821 population. The Intendencia de Durango or Nueva Vizcaya (383.074 km² vector; 381.498,3 km² grid) fell from 130k in 1570 to 95k in 1646 before doubling to 110k in 1742, 122,9k in 1793, 159,7k in 1803 and 195k in 1821 (0,51 inhabitants per km² documentary; 0,46 gridded), anchored by Durango (14k), Chihuahua (11,6k, born from the Santa Eulalia silver strikes of 1707) and Parral [@Gerhard1993; @Humboldt1811]. Across the Sierra Madre Occidental, the Intendencia de Arizpe (Sonora-Sinaloa) and Baja California (368.878 km² vector; 408.887,6 km² grid) experienced protracted indigenous contraction across its Jesuit and post-1767 Franciscan mission chains—falling from 165k in 1570 to 115k in 1646 and 98k in 1742—before silver mining at Álamos, Rosario and Copala (6,5k) and agricultural settlement around Culiacán (10,8k) lifted it to 102k in 1793, 130,4k in 1803 and 155k in 1821 (0,42 inhabitants per km² documentary; 0,86 gridded) [@Gerhard1993]. Finally, the Provincias Internas de Oriente—Coahuila, Nuevo León and José de Escandón's post-1748 colonisation of Nuevo Santander (Tamaulipas), covering 291.898 km² vector (298.122,2 km² grid)—more than trebled after 1646 from 55k to 72k in 1742, 105k in 1793, 142k in 1803 and 175k in 1821 (0,60 inhabitants per km² documentary; 0,51 gridded), anchored by Saltillo (14,5k) and Monterrey (11k) [@Gerhard1993; @Bustamante1991Matter].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Structure Across New Spain

Unlike pre-urban Mesoamerican frontiers or rural agrarian empires with a single capital and few intermediate towns, late-colonial New Spain possessed a mature, well-integrated urban hierarchy spanning silver *reales*, textile cities, regional *audiencia* capitals, Atlantic ports and hundreds of parish towns [@MinoGrijalva2001; @Brading1971]. Figure \ref{fig:new-spain-hierarchy} plots the 12 largest recorded settlements (Panel A) alongside the log-log rank-size curve across all 826 catalogued settlements (Panel B). Fitting a power-law regression to the upper 180 settlements yields a Zipf exponent of $\alpha = 0,67$ ($R^2 = 0,99$). That moderately shallow slope—well below unity—reflects New Spain's dual urban architecture: towering administrative primacy in Mexico City (179,8k, roughly 2,55 times larger than Guanajuato at 70,6k and 2,65 times Puebla at 67,8k), balanced by an exceptionally broad second and third tier of commercial, mining and diocesan centres between 15k and 40k inhabitants (Guadalajara at 40k, Mérida at 36k, Querétaro at 35k, Zacatecas at 33k, Oaxaca at 24k, León at 21,4k, Valladolid at 21k, Campeche at 19,5k, San Luis Potosí at 19k and San Miguel el Grande at 18,2k) [@MinoGrijalva2001; @Humboldt1811].

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/viceroyalty_of_new_spain_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Largest recorded settlements in the Viceroyalty of New Spain (Panel A) and log-log settlement rank-size distribution across 826 catalogued locales showing a power-law fit across the upper 180 entries ($\\alpha = 0,67$, $R^2 = 0,99$, Panel B), 1535 to 1821.",
  "fig:new-spain-hierarchy"
)
```

Table \ref{tab:top-cities} tabulates the top 20 settlements recorded in the chapter summary register, pairing peak population and year with geographic coordinates, intendancy assignment and multi-year observation depth. A sharp structural distinction emerges between multi-census urban cores—such as Mexico City (9 observations from 1570 to 1820), Guadalajara (10), Oaxaca (10), Puebla (7), Querétaro (7), Zacatecas (7) and Guanajuato (6)—and single-year 1778 or 1780 ecclesiastical *curato* (parish jurisdiction) counts from the archdioceses of México and Guadalajara, such as Actopan (25,8k in 1778), Lagos (22,2k in 1780), Encarnación (19,2k in 1780) and Sierra de Pinos (18,1k in 1780), whose totals encompass both the parish seat and surrounding dependent *haciendas* and *ranchos* [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Sanchez2000Algunas].

```{r tab-top-cities, results='asis'}
top_list <- summary_cache$settlement_stats$top_settlements
fmt_c <- function(v) viscount_fmt_number(round(as.numeric(v), 2L), 2L)

top_rows <- lapply(top_list, function(e) {
  nm <- as.character(e$name)
  key <- paste0(nm, "-", as.character(e$country))
  full_e <- sett_data[[key]]
  rid <- if (!is.null(full_e) && !is.null(full_e$region_id)) as.character(full_e$region_id) else ""
  reg_lbl <- if (rid %in% names(reg_lookup)) reg_lookup[[rid]] else rid
  n_obs <- if (!is.null(full_e) && !is.null(full_e$population)) length(full_e$population) else 1L
  data.frame(
    City = nm,
    Subregion = reg_lbl,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_c(e$lat), ", ", fmt_c(e$lon)),
    Year = as.character(as.integer(e$peak_year)),
    Peak = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(e$peak_pop), 0L),
    Obs = as.character(n_obs),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
rownames(df_top) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Top 20 settlements and parish centres in the Viceroyalty of New Spain ordered by peak recorded population, 1535 to 1821.",
  c("Settlement", "Intendancy or Province", "Lat, Lon", "Peak Year", "Peak Pop.", "Obs."),
  list(label = "tab:top-cities", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four archival and methodological constraints qualify demographic reconstruction across colonial New Spain.

First, every colonial enumeration suffered from structural under-registration and fiscal evasion. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century *tasaciones de tributos* omitted exempt *caciques*, young adults and mobile *indios laboríos* who fled home villages onto haciendas and mining camps [@Zevallos1999Movimento; @Fernandez2023Epidemias]. Even the landmark 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo Census went unfinished in Guadalajara, Veracruz and Coahuila, provoked widespread hiding by families fearing Bourbon militia conscription and routinely under-counted female employment and single-headed households in urban tenements [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Cervantescortes2021Registro; @Hidalgo2024Michoaca]. While Humboldt's 1803 upward adjustment of 10% to 15% corrects the gross bias, province-level margins of error remain roughly $\pm 10\%$ for 1793 to 1821 and $\pm 15\%$ to $\pm 20\%$ for 1570 to 1742 [@Humboldt1811; @CookBorah1971].

Second, spatial coverage inside the 826-site settlement gazetteer reflects the uneven survival of regional colonial padrones rather than uniform historical urbanisation. Because Stangl's HGIS de las Indias incorporates Bishop Tamarón y Romeral's exhaustive 1765 northern visitation (419 records) and Sánchez Santiró's 1778 Archdiocese of México padrones (242 records), the frontier provinces of Arizpe (230 catalogued sites) and Durango (214) together with México (205) account for 78,6% of all settlement entries. By contrast, Oaxaca—home to over 534k people in 1803—registers just 1 urban entry (Antequera) because its overwhelmingly rural indigenous *pueblos* were tallied by administrative *partido* rather than nucleated city censuses. Furthermore, several 1778 and 1780 parish entries (such as Actopan, Lagos and Encarnación) combine town cores with rural parish *haciendas*, while two overlapping census syntheses list Michoacán's capital under both Valladolid (21k in 1805) and Valladolid Michoacán (18k in 1803) at identical coordinates, and boundary-edge alignment places Tuxtla Gutiérrez inside the Veracruz isthmian polygon rather than Guatemala's Chiapas jurisdiction.

Third, reconciling documentary intendancy aggregates (6,53M in 1821) against the continuous spatial-kriging substratum (4,57M in 1820) exposes an appreciable late-colonial scale gap of roughly 25% to 30%. On the gridded surface, a discrete administrative-weight shift between 1770 and 1780 also transfers apparent density sharply into México, Puebla and Guanajuato while reducing northern frontier gridded cells. Readers interpreting long-run growth rates should therefore anchor macroeconomic and provincial ratios to the documentary intendancy ledger (Tables \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} and \ref{tab:hgis-intendancies}), using the gridded surface (Figure \ref{fig:new-spain-trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:gridded-trajectory}) strictly for intra-provincial spatial allocation and decadal shock timing.

Fourth, *casta* categories and northern frontier indigenous populations defy rigid retrospective tabulation. Archival and bio-anthropological research confirms that colonial ethnic labels shifted across a person's life course and masked extensive tri-continental—and on the Pacific coast, Asian—admixture [@Bustamante1991Matter; @Healy2017Social; @Rodriguezrodriguez2021Admixture]. Likewise, autonomous Apache, Comanche, Seri and Yaqui bands living beyond Spanish *presidios* and missions in Sonora, Chihuahua and Coahuila remained outside parish registers throughout 1535 to 1821, ensuring that northern frontier benchmarks represent conservative floors of true human occupancy [@Gerhard1993; @Contributors2018High].

# Conclusion

Across the 286 years between the establishment of the Viceroyalty of New Spain in 1535 and Mexican Independence in 1821, colonial Mexico underwent one of the earliest and most consequential demographic recoveries in the post-contact Americas. Rebounding from a mid-seventeenth-century nadir of 2,09M in 1646 after the catastrophic epidemics of the sixteenth century, the viceroyalty expanded more than threefold to 3,23M in 1742, 4,53M in the 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo horizon, 5,84M to 5,90M in Humboldt's 1803 tables and 6,53M at Independence in 1821 [@CookBorah1971; @Gerhard1962; @SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811]. Even severe late-colonial Malthusian shocks—the 1736 to 1739 *matlazáhuatl* pandemic, the 1785 to 1786 Year of Hunger and eleven years of destructive insurgency between 1810 and 1821—checked rather than reversed that long-run upward trajectory [@RabellRomero1990; @Brading1971; @Ficker2025Mineri].

Just as enduring as the aggregate recovery was the geographic and social transformation it forged. While the Mesoamerican core of México, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Oaxaca remained populous and culturally resilient, sustained migration, silver mining and commercial estate agriculture propelled the Bajío and Nueva Galicia to the forefront of colonial growth, lifting Guanajuato to the highest provincial density in New Spain and embedding an urban network of 826 catalogued towns led by Mexico City (179,8k), Guanajuato (70,6k), Puebla (67,8k) and Guadalajara (40k) [@Brading1971; @MinoGrijalva2001; @Sanchez2000Algunas]. Out of the interplay of indigenous communal survival, European settlement, African plantation and urban labour and Pacific admixture emerged the regional demographic architecture—sharp contrasts between dense central-western corridors, indigenous southern highlands and sparsely peopled northern steppes—that independent Mexico inherited in 1821 and that continues to shape national sub-regional fertility and mortality patterns into the twenty-first century [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Rodriguezrodriguez2021Admixture; @Contributors2023Adolescence; @Contributors2018High].

# Appendix

## Gridded Substratum Decadal Series (1600 to 1820)

Table \ref{tab:gridded-trajectory} compiles the continuous spatial-kriging substratum across all 12 sub-regions from 1600 to 1820 (total raster footprint 1.965.350 km²), paired with 1820 gridded densities and catalogued settlement counts per polygon. Comparing this table with the documentary intendancy ledger in Table \ref{tab:subregion-benchmarks} illustrates both the 1770 to 1780 Bourbon boundary re-weighting step and the 1810 insurgency contraction from 4,25M to 4,08M.

```{r tab-gridded-trajectory, results='asis'}
sc_cov <- ledger_data$saturation_audit$submask_coverage

g_rows <- lapply(subregions_grid, function(r) {
  rid <- as.character(r$id)
  tr <- r$trajectory
  sc_v <- if (!is.null(sc_cov[[rid]])) as.integer(sc_cov[[rid]]) else 0L
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    P1600 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1600"]])),
    P1700 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1700"]])),
    P1740 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1740"]])),
    P1780 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1780"]])),
    P1800 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1800"]])),
    P1810 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1810"]])),
    P1820 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tr[["1820"]])),
    Dens20 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(r$end_density_km2), 2L),
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(sc_v, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_grid <- do.call(rbind, g_rows)
dtr <- summary_cache$domain_trajectory
df_grid <- rbind(
  df_grid,
  data.frame(
    Subregion = "Gridded Domain Total",
    P1600 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1600"]])),
    P1700 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1700"]])),
    P1740 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1740"]])),
    P1780 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1780"]])),
    P1800 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1800"]])),
    P1810 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1810"]])),
    P1820 = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(dtr[["1820"]])),
    Dens20 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(dtr[["1820"]]) / grid_area, 2L),
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
)
rownames(df_grid) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_grid,
  "Gridded spatial-kriging population trajectories (1600 to 1820), 1820 gridded densities (inhabitants per km²) and catalogued settlement counts across 12 sub-regions.",
  c("Sub-Region", "1600", "1700", "1740", "1780", "1800", "1810", "1820", "1820 Dens.", "Sites"),
  list(label = "tab:gridded-trajectory", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Gazetteer Provenance and Saturation Waves

Table \ref{tab:provenance-summary} summarises the four-wave source-ledger saturation audit alongside the primary source classes underpinning all 826 catalogued settlements (with 0% crowd-sourced fallback).

```{r tab-provenance-summary, results='asis'}
waves <- ledger_data$saturation_audit$waves
w_labels <- c(
  primary_official_national_censuses_and_archival_registers = "Official Censuses and Archival Registers",
  verified_peer_reviewed_demographic_papers_and_monographs = "Peer-Reviewed Historical Demography Monographs",
  longitudinal_census_and_archaeological_survey_backfill = "Longitudinal Census Backfill",
  subregion_gap_hunter_verification_sweep = "Sub-Regional Gap Audit Sweep"
)
w_rows <- lapply(waves, function(w) {
  cls_k <- as.character(w$source_class)
  lbl <- if (cls_k %in% names(w_labels)) w_labels[[cls_k]] else cls_k
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", as.integer(w$wave)),
    SourceClass = lbl,
    Prior = viscount_fmt_number(as.integer(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    Added = viscount_fmt_number(as.integer(w$newly_included), 0L),
    Gain = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$marginal_gain_pct), 2L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_waves <- do.call(rbind, w_rows)
rownames(df_waves) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_waves,
  "Four-wave gazetteer saturation ledger across 826 included colonial Mexican settlements (33 duplicate or out-of-bounds candidates excluded; 0% crowd share).",
  c("Wave", "Source Corpus Class", "Prior Total", "Newly Included", "Marginal Gain"),
  list(label = "tab:provenance-summary", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Footnotes

1. **Villaseñor y Sánchez's 1742 *familias* conversion:** In *Theatro Americano* (1746 to 1748), José Antonio de Villaseñor y Sánchez reported provincial populations in *familias* (households) rather than individual heads. Following Peter Gerhard's parish-by-parish audit in *México en 1742*, multipliers of 4,2 to 5,0 persons per household yield a viceregal total of roughly 3,23M inhabitants across the 12 intendancies and frontier provinces [@Gerhard1962].
2. **Revillagigedo Census under-enumeration and Humboldt's 1803 adjustment:** The 1790 to 1793 Revillagigedo Census left returns unfinished for Guadalajara, Veracruz and Coahuila and suffered widespread evasion linked to military militia levies. Alexander von Humboldt applied a 10% to 15% under-registration correction plus ten years of natural increase to raise the 1793 twelve-intendancy subtotal of 4.367.703 (4,48M to 4,53M with frontier provinces) to 5.837.100 (5,84M) in 1803 [@SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811].
3. **Eighteenth-century mortality shocks:** Parish burial series compiled by Cecilia Rabell Romero, David Brading and Lilia Oliver Sánchez confirm two viceroyalty-wide demographic crises during the eighteenth century: the 1736 to 1739 *matlazáhuatl* pandemic (roughly 150k to 200k deaths) and the 1785 to 1786 *Año del Hambre* harvest failure and typhus outbreak (roughly 300k deaths) [@RabellRomero1990; @Brading1971; @Sanchez2000Algunas].
4. **Gazetteer parish-vs-city scope notes:** Within the 826-entry colonial settlement register, several 1778 Archdiocese of México and 1780 Bishopric of Guadalajara entries (notably Actopan at 25.811, Lagos at 22.184, Encarnación at 19.200 and Sierra de Pinos at 18.062) report *curato* (parish jurisdiction) headcounts including dependent *haciendas* and *ranchos*. Two separate archival series for Michoacán's capital—Valladolid (21.000 in 1805) and Valladolid Michoacán (18.000 in 1803)—remain preserved distinctly in the source register to maintain strict provenance traceability.
